message.content:
The total number of distinct positions that can arise in a standard game of chess (starting from the initial arrangement and following all legal moves) is astronomically large.  It is commonly quoted as roughly

\[
10^{43}\text{–}10^{46}
\]

positions.  

A more precise estimate, based on exhaustive enumeration of legal positions, puts the figure at about \(10^{46}\).  This is often referred to as the “Shannon number” (after Claude Shannon), which gives a lower bound on the complexity of chess.  In short, there are on the order of tens of quadrillion quadrillion (i.e., \(10^{46}\)) possible arrangements.
